title: FRM Liquidity, Lesson 6: Market liquidity and funding liquidity
subtitle: Two different kinds of liquidity, and the spiral in which they drain each other
whyItMatters: Almost every financial crisis travels through the liquidity channel. Telling the two kinds apart is the precondition for understanding how an institution that is well capitalised on paper can still collapse within days.
openingQuestion: How does market liquidity differ from funding liquidity?
openingOptions: Selling fast without moving the price, versus being able to raise cash
Market liquidity applies to equities while funding liquidity applies to bonds
Market liquidity is set by the central bank, funding liquidity by the market
They are the same idea, named differently in developed and emerging markets
explanation: There are two kinds of liquidity and they belong to two different subjects. Market liquidity is a property of an asset: can it be sold quickly, and how much price is lost in a hurried sale. Funding liquidity is a property of an institution: can it raise the cash to meet obligations as they fall due. What makes them dangerous is the feedback loop between them - a cash shortage forces asset sales, forced sales push prices down, falling prices erode collateral value and make borrowing harder still.

diagram.label: Funding is withdrawn → a funding liquidity shortage
Assets must be sold to raise cash
The fire sale pushes prices down → market liquidity deteriorates
Falling prices devalue collateral → more funding is pulled

realWorldExample.company: The liquidity spiral in market stress episodes
realWorldExample.description: The pattern repeats across many stress episodes: an institution comes under suspicion, its short-term funding is not rolled, and it has to sell assets for cash. The selling pushes prices down, which reduces the collateral value held by that institution and by everyone else holding similar assets, triggering further margin calls and further selling pressure. The two kinds of liquidity drain each other along an amplifying loop.

quiz.question: Why can an institution with a healthy capital ratio still fail because of liquidity?
options: Because capital ratios stop being recognised during a crisis
Because capital measures loss absorption, not cash on hand
Because shareholders' equity automatically converts into debt
Because well-capitalised firms always face heavier withdrawals
quiz.explanation: Capital and liquidity answer two different questions: are there more assets than liabilities, and is there enough cash to pay what falls due tomorrow morning. A perfectly healthy balance sheet made entirely of long-dated assets still cannot repay a deposit that is withdrawn today. Capital ratios remain valid measures in a crisis, equity does not convert into debt, and a strong capital position tends to slow withdrawals rather than accelerate them.

quiz.question: How is the liquidity cost of an asset usually measured?
options: By the time remaining until the asset reaches its maturity date
By the dividend yield the asset pays each year to its holder
By the bid-ask spread and the price impact of selling in size
By the credit rating assigned to the issuer of that asset
quiz.explanation: There are two components: the bid-ask spread is a cost even on a small order, while price impact is the extra cost that appears once the size exceeds the depth of the order book. For a large position the second component is usually much bigger than the first. Maturity, dividend yield and issuer rating all describe other properties of the asset entirely and none of them tells you what a hurried sale would cost.

quiz.question: Why is liquidity risk harder to hedge with derivatives than market risk is?
options: Because liquidity risk always causes small losses, so hedging is unnecessary
Because no derivative contract on liquidity exists to trade
Because supervisors forbid the use of derivatives for liquidity management
Because it erupts exactly when the counterparty is in trouble too
quiz.explanation: Hedging depends on a counterparty willing to take on the risk. A liquidity crisis is systemic, so at the exact moment you need to exercise your claim the counterparty is short of cash as well - which is why liquidity defence rests on self-held reserves rather than on contracts. Liquidity losses can be fatal rather than small, contracts referencing liquidity conditions do exist, and no supervisor bans hedging for this purpose.

quiz.question: How does the spiral between the two kinds of liquidity operate?
options: A cash shortage forces sales, sales cut prices, lower prices make borrowing harder
Losing market liquidity raises rates, and higher rates raise capital cost
Investors pull out, the share price falls, and a downgrade follows
The central bank tightens policy, making both kinds of liquidity scarce
quiz.explanation: This is the mechanism that brought down several institutions in the 2008 crisis: each turn makes the next one worse, and it runs on its own without any fresh shock arriving. Falling collateral values also trigger additional margin calls, tightening the loop by one more notch. The other three describe real effects, but each is a one-way chain rather than a self-reinforcing loop between funding and market liquidity.

quiz.question: Why must high-quality liquid assets be free of any pledge to another borrowing?
options: Because accounting rules bar pledged assets from the balance sheet
Because a pledged asset cannot be sold for cash when needed
Because pledged assets attract a materially higher haircut
Because the pledgee has the right to repurchase it at market price
quiz.explanation: A large portfolio of government bonds is no help at all if every one of them already sits inside a repurchase agreement. This is why liquidity standards count only the portion that is genuinely free and convertible into cash immediately. Pledged assets stay on the balance sheet under accounting rules, the haircut is a pricing detail rather than the reason, and a pledgee holds security rather than a repurchase right.

practicePrompt.question: An institution has a capital ratio of 16%, well above the minimum, but cannot roll a repo maturing this week. What is happening?
options: Well capitalised but short of liquidity - two different questions
The 16% capital ratio must have been miscalculated somewhere
High capital always means funding is available, so this is an error
A liquidity shortage always produces a capital shortage immediately
practicePrompt.explanation: Capital measures the ability to ABSORB LOSS: how much buffer remains before assets fail to cover liabilities. Liquidity measures the ability to PAY ON TIME: is there cash today for today's obligations. An institution can be very comfortable on the first question and default on the second, because its assets are long-dated while its obligations fall due this week. That is where the spiral begins: if funding cannot be rolled you have to sell assets, selling into a weak market pushes prices down, lower prices mean higher haircuts and other counterparties pull away too - and only then does the 16% capital ratio start genuinely eroding.

keyTakeaways: Market liquidity belongs to the asset, funding liquidity belongs to the institution
Capital measures loss absorption, liquidity measures the ability to pay what falls due - two different questions
Liquidity cost comprises the bid-ask spread plus the price impact of selling in size
Liquidity risk is hard to hedge with derivatives because it is systemic

summary.keyIdea: The two kinds of liquidity amplify each other: a cash shortage forces asset sales, the fire sale worsens prices and that pulls further funding away
summary.commonMistake: Treating a good capital ratio as evidence of liquidity safety
summary.action: For every portfolio, ask two separate questions: how fast can this asset be sold and at what price, and how quickly could its funding be withdrawn

application.title: Applying it to personal finance
application.message: The same logic applies to a personal portfolio: your total assets may be very large, but if they all sit in property then one unexpected expense still forces you into expensive borrowing.
application.secondary: This is exactly why an emergency fund has to be held in highly liquid assets.

sections.text: Capital and liquidity are usually lumped together in everyday conversation, but they answer two entirely different questions - and institutions fail on the second one far more often.

left.label: Market liquidity
left.text: A property of the asset: how much size can be sold, how quickly, and how much price is given up against the reference level.

right.label: Funding liquidity
right.text: A property of the institution: whether it can raise or retain the funding needed to meet obligations as they fall due.

sections.text: When short-term funding is not rolled, the institution is forced to sell assets. Selling under duress pushes prices down, which lowers collateral values, which triggers further margin calls and further suspicion from funding providers. Each turn of the loop makes the next one heavier.

sections.label: Why a contract cannot hedge it
sections.text: Market risk can be hedged because there is always a counterparty willing to take the opposite position. A liquidity crisis is systemic: at the exact moment you need cash, everyone else needs it too. Liquidity defence therefore rests on self-held reserves and on maturity structure, not on a contract with somebody else.
Measuring market liquidity with three numbers rather than a feeling

sections.title: What a bond quoted at 99.80 / 100.20 is telling you
sections.subtitle: All three dimensions deteriorate at once when markets tighten, so measuring one is not enough

concepts.def: 0.40 on a price of 100, which is 40 basis points. Selling immediately means giving up about that much against the mid. This is the cost of a small order, and the only dimension visible on the screen.

If there are only 2 million of buyers at 99.80 and you need to sell 10 million, the rest has to walk down to lower price levels. The real cost of a large order is not 40 basis points but a great deal more, and it does not appear on the quote line.

How long the order book takes to refill after a large order has gone through. A market that recovers quickly lets you keep selling; one that recovers slowly makes your second order more expensive than your first.

sections.label: Why watching only the bid-ask spread fails at the worst moment
sections.text: In a crisis, bid-ask spreads usually widen fairly modestly while depth evaporates. The screen still shows a price that looks acceptable, but the size standing behind it is close to zero. An institution that sizes its selling capacity from the observed spread will believe it can liquidate its portfolio near market prices - and will discover the opposite on precisely the day it matters most.

lines: Capital keeps an institution alive in accounting terms; liquidity keeps it alive until tomorrow morning.
